chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Aban, from Al-Halbi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who confessed to a hadd penalty upon himself, then denied it afterwards. He (peace be upon him) said: 'When he confesses in the presence of the Imam that he stole, then denies, his hand is cut off, even if his nose is crushed (i.e., despite his haughtiness). If he confesses that he drank wine, or by accusation, they lash him eighty lashes.' I said: 'If he confesses to a hadd in which stoning is obligatory, would you stone him?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'No, but I would lash him with the hadd.'

key_terms.رَغِمَ أَنْفُهُ: His nose was crushed (idiom for despite haughtiness)
key_terms.ضَارِبَهُ الْحَدَّ: I would lash him with the penalty

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling when a person confesses to a hadd crime and then denies it?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the judicial principle that a self-confession to a hadd crime remains valid even if the confessor later retracts, ensuring the penalty is executed. It specifically distinguishes between lesser hadd crimes like theft and drinking, where the physical penalty is applied regardless of denial, and stoning (rajm), where the Imam opts for lashes to avoid the finality of death in case of error. This reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on caution (ihtiyat) in applying capital punishment, prioritizing the preservation of life when certainty is not absolute.
